bib.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
bib.venue: NeurIPS 2023 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks (arXiv v4, 24 Dec 2023)

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed; appendix B case-study chat transcripts (Figs 11-16) skimmed, not read line by line.

question: Can strong LLMs act as judges that match human preferences when evaluating open-ended, multi-turn chat assistants, and what biases limit them?
hypothesis: Strong LLMs such as GPT-4, being RLHF-trained, already align with humans, so their judgments can match human-human agreement once position, verbosity and reasoning limits are mitigated.
contributions: Human preference datasets with high-quality questions and diverse user interactions from MT-bench and Chatbot Arena (80 MT-bench questions, 3K expert votes, 30K conversations with human preferences)

method.summary: Builds MT-bench (80 two-turn questions, 8 categories) and Chatbot Arena (crowdsourced anonymous battles), collects human votes, and measures agreement of GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and Claude-v1 judges (pairwise, single-answer, reference-guided) with humans. Probes position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases and math grading, and evaluates Vicuna/LLaMA/Alpaca variants with MMLU, TruthfulQA and MT-bench.
method.task: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation of chat assistants against human preference

datasets.name: MT-bench
datasets.size: 80 questions (8 categories x 10 two-turn questions); about 3K expert votes
datasets.source: Manually designed by the authors; categories writing, roleplay, extraction, reasoning, math, coding, knowledge I (STEM), knowledge II (humanities/social science)
datasets.preprocessing: Answers generated for all 80 questions by 6 models; each of 58 expert labelers judged at least 20 random multi-turn questions

datasets.name: Chatbot Arena
datasets.size: about 30K votes after one month; 3K single-turn votes randomly sampled for agreement
datasets.source: Crowdsourced anonymous battles, 2114 unique IPs in the 3K sample; users accepted terms allowing release
datasets.preprocessing: PII to be cleaned and toxic conversations tagged with OpenAI moderation API before release

datasets.name: ShareGPT conversations (Vicuna training data)
datasets.size: 125K conversations after cleaning; All 370M tokens / 257K sequences; Single 184M tokens / 257K; Selected 4.8M tokens / 3K sequences
datasets.preprocessing: HTML to markdown, drop low-quality samples, split long conversations to fit context; Selected = centroids of 3K clusters of sequences with at least 3 GPT-4 turns

datasets.name: Arena votes for judge fine-tuning (Appendix F)
datasets.split: 20K/2K; tested on the same 3K Arena set as the main body
datasets.preprocessing: Three-way labels A, B, tie (tie includes both-bad)

training.objective: Vicuna: supervised fine-tuning on ShareGPT conversations (inferred: standard SFT, code built on Alpaca code with multi-turn handling). Judge: 3-way sequence classification (A, B, tie).
training.lr_schedule: cosine for the fine-tuned judge; not stated for Vicuna
training.tokens: Vicuna-7B Selected 4.8M, Single 184M, All 370M training tokens (Table 8/14)
training.hardware: 8x A100 GPUs, SkyPilot managed spot instances, FlashAttention
training.wall_clock: longest single training run around 2 days

inference.temperature: 0.7 when generating the two similar answers per first-turn question for the position-bias test; judge temperature not stated
inference.samples: Each question answered by 6 models (MT-bench); position test uses one pair of GPT-3.5 answers per first-turn question; swap-order judge called twice; number of judge runs/seeds not stated
inference.prompting: Zero-shot default; pairwise, single-answer (1-10), reference-guided and CoT variants; multi-turn shows full conversations in one prompt; few-shot (3 examples) tested but not default

parameters.swap_rule: declare a win only when the answer is preferred in both orders, otherwise tie
parameters.few_shot_examples: 3 (A better, B better, tie), made with GPT-3.5 and Vicuna answers and GPT-4 judgments; makes API calls 4x more expensive
parameters.single_answer_scoring: score each turn on scale of 10, average over 160 = 80x2 turns

metrics.name: Agreement
metrics.definition: probability that randomly selected (non-identical) individuals of each judge type agree on a randomly selected question; S1 counts ties and inconsistent as tie (random 33%), S2 non-tie only (random 50%)

metrics.name: Consistency (position bias)
metrics.definition: percentage of cases where a judge gives consistent results when swapping the order of two assistants

metrics.name: Average win rate
metrics.definition: average of win rates against all other players, with or without ties

metrics.name: MT-bench score
metrics.definition: GPT-4 single-answer score on 1-10 scale, averaged over 160 turns

eval.protocol: 58 expert human labelers (graduate students) on MT-bench; crowd votes on Arena; LLM judges evaluate all pairs; no seeds or significance tests stated.

availability.data: MT-bench questions, 3K expert votes, 30K conversations with human preferences, same repo

prompts.text:
[System]
Please act as an impartial judge and evaluate the quality of the response provided by an AI assistant to the user question displayed below. Your evaluation should consider factors such as the helpfulness, relevance, accuracy, depth, creativity, and level of detail of the response. Begin your evaluation by providing a short explanation. Be as objective as possible. After providing your explanation, please rate the response on a scale of 1 to 10 by strictly following this format: "[[rating]]", for example: "Rating: [[5]]".
[Question]
{question}
[The Start of Assistant’s Answer]
{answer}
[The End of Assistant’s Answer]

prompts.purpose: Chain-of-thought judge for math and reasoning
prompts.text: You should independently solve the user question step-by-step first. Then compare both assistants’ answers with your answer. Identify and correct any mistakes. (rest as Figure 5; full text in Figure 7)
You will be given a reference answer, assistant A’s answer, and assistant B’s answer. (full text in Figure 8; reference answer inserted as [The Start of Reference Answer] {answer_ref})

prompts.purpose: Multi-turn pairwise and reference-guided single-answer prompts
prompts.text: <|The Start of Assistant A’s Conversation with User|> ### User: {question 1} ### Assistant A: {answer 1} ### User: {question 2} ### Assistant A: {answer 2} (full text Figures 9 and 10)

results.claim: GPT-4 pairwise judge agrees with human experts on non-tie MT-bench first-turn votes at 85%, above the 81% human-human agreement.
results.setup: MT-bench, 6 models, 58 expert labelers, setup S2 non-tie votes, first turn, GPT-4 default zero-shot pairwise prompt
results.quote: The agreement under setup S2 (w/o tie) between GPT-4 and humans reaches 85%, which is even higher than the agreement among humans (81%).
results.note: Intro text cites this as Table 4, but the agreement table is Table 5.

results.claim: Under setup S1 (ties and inconsistent counted as ties), GPT-4 pairwise agrees with humans only 66%, vs 63% human-human.
results.table: Table 5(a), row G4-Pair, column S1 Human (66%, 1343 votes); row Human, column S1 Human (63%, 721)

results.claim: Chatbot Arena: GPT-4 pairwise agrees with crowd humans at 87% on non-tie votes (64% S1).
results.setup: 3K single-turn Arena votes, 2114 unique IPs, S2 non-tie
results.table: Table 6, row G4, column S2 H (87%, 1944)

results.claim: Humans deemed GPT-4's judgments reasonable in 75% of disagreement cases and changed their choice in 34%.
results.setup: MT-bench data collection, shown only when human differed from GPT-4
results.quote: humans deemed GPT-4’s judgments reasonable in 75% of cases and are even willing to change their choices in 34% of cases.

results.claim: Position bias is strong: only GPT-4 is consistent in more than 60% of swapped cases; Claude-v1 is 23.8% consistent with default prompt.
results.n: inferred: 80 pairs from the 80 MT-bench first-turn questions
results.setup: Two near-identical GPT-3.5 answers (temperature 0.7) per first-turn MT-bench question, default prompt
results.table: Table 2, row GPT-4 default, column Consistency
results.note: Claude-v1 biased toward first 75.0%, GPT-3.5 50.0%, GPT-4 30.0%; Claude-v1 shows a name bias toward 'Assistant A' under the rename prompt.

results.claim: Verbosity attack ('repetitive list') fools Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 91.3% of the time but GPT-4 only 8.7%.
results.setup: 23 MT-bench answers with numbered lists, list rephrased by GPT-4 and prepended; success if judge prefers the padded answer
results.table: Table 3, column GPT-4, row Failure rate

results.claim: Reference-guided judging cuts GPT-4 math grading failure from 14/20 (default) to 3/20.
results.setup: LLaMA-13B vs Vicuna-13B on 10 math questions with positions swapped; failure = GPT-4 says an incorrect answer is correct
results.quote: In Table 4, we see a significant improvement in failure rate (from 70% to 15%) over the default prompt.

results.claim: Few-shot judge raises GPT-4 consistency from 65.0% to 77.5% but makes API calls 4x more expensive.
results.quote: the few-shot judge can significantly increase the consistency of GPT-4 from 65.0% to 77.5%.
results.note: Few-shot GPT-4 agreement with humans on MT-bench is similar to zero-shot (Appendix D.2).

results.claim: Self-enhancement bias is suggestive but not established: GPT-4 favours itself with a 10% higher win rate, Claude-v1 25%, GPT-3.5 does not favour itself.
results.setup: Six models on MT-bench, win rate w/o tie, judges vs humans (Fig 3b)
results.quote: GPT-4 favors itself with a 10% higher win rate; Claude-v1 favors itself with a 25% higher win rate.
results.note: Authors state their study cannot determine whether self-enhancement bias exists.

results.claim: Agreement between GPT-4 and humans rises with the win-rate gap between the two models, from 70% to nearly 100%.
results.setup: Per model pair, non-tie votes, MT-bench (Fig 2)
results.quote: the agreement between GPT-4 and human progressively increases in line with the performance disparity of the model pairs (i.e., larger win rate difference), from 70% to nearly 100%.

results.claim: Position bias is larger for close model pairs and nearly vanishes for distant pairs (GPT-3.5 vs LLaMA-13B 98.8% consistent).
results.setup: GPT-4 default prompt on three model pairs
results.table: Table 11, row GPT-3.5 vs LLaMA-13B, column Consistent

results.claim: Position bias is highest on writing, STEM and humanities and lowest on math and coding (86.0% consistent).
results.setup: GPT-4 default prompt by MT-bench category

results.claim: Fine-tuning Vicuna-13B on Arena votes as a 3-way classifier lifts position consistency from 16.2% to 65.0% and gives 85.5% non-tie agreement (56.8% with ties).
results.setup: 20K train votes, 3 epochs, cosine schedule, 2e-5 max lr; 2K validation
results.quote: It achieves 56.8% when including all three labels, and 85.5% when excluding tie predictions and labels
results.note: Zero-shot Vicuna-13B has consistency 11.2-16.2% and error rate 22.5-78.8%.

results.claim: Vicuna-13B (all) scores 6.39 on MT-bench vs GPT-3.5 7.94 and GPT-4 8.99, and 52.1 on MMLU 5-shot vs 70.0 and 86.4.
results.setup: GPT-4 single-answer grading, average over 80 questions x 2 turns
results.table: Table 8, row Vicuna-13B (all), column MT-Bench Score (GPT-4)

results.claim: A 3K-conversation (4.8M-token) SFT set teaches GPT-4-preferred style (MT-bench 5.95) without improving MMLU (37.3 vs LLaMA-7B 35.2), so one benchmark cannot determine model quality.
results.table: Table 8, row Vicuna-7B (selected), column MT-Bench Score (GPT-4)

results.claim: GPT-4 single-answer grading matches pairwise GPT-4 and humans well (84-85% S2 with humans) while being more scalable, but gives more ties.
results.setup: MT-bench first turn, G4-Single vs Human, S2
results.table: Table 5(a), row G4-Single, column S2 Human (85%, 739)

limits: Authors: the paper emphasizes helpfulness but largely neglects safety (honesty and harmlessness).
Authors: multiple helpfulness dimensions (accuracy, relevance, creativity) are collapsed into a single metric.
Authors: due to limited data and small differences, the study cannot determine whether self-enhancement bias exists; controlled study is hard.
Authors: high consistency from few-shot examples may not imply accuracy, and few-shot may introduce new biases.
Authors: case studies use gpt-4-0314 and may not be reproducible with future GPT-4 versions.
Position-bias, verbosity (23 answers) and math (10 questions, 20 trials) tests are small samples; no confidence intervals or significance tests reported.
Agreement is for GPT-4 only at 80+%; Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 are weaker, and the reported rates depend on tie handling (S1 66% vs S2 85%).
MT-bench has only 80 questions; judge model versions and decoding temperature for judging are not stated.
Closed-source judges (GPT-4, Claude-v1, GPT-3.5) have since been superseded; results are from early-2023 models.

terms.definition: using strong LLMs, such as GPT-4, as a surrogate for humans to evaluate chat assistants
when an LLM exhibits a propensity to favor certain positions over others
when an LLM judge favors longer, verbose responses, even if they are not as clear, high-quality, or accurate as shorter alternatives
the effect that LLM judges may favor the answers generated by themselves
the probability of randomly selected (but not identical) individuals of each type agreeing on a randomly selected question
the judge first answers independently, then that answer is shown as a reference answer in the judge prompt
